title: Nouns II — The Plural
summary: The seven formations a German plural is built with, the Umlaut that accompanies three of them, the endings that never take it, and the reason a noun is cited with its plural rather than derived from a rule.

rules.heading: The seven plural formations
rules.statement: German builds the plural of a noun in seven ways: with no change, with the Umlaut alone, with **-e**, with **-e** and the Umlaut, with **-er**, with **-(e)n**, and with **-s**. All seven take the one article **die** (¶26).

sources.citation: Durrell, Martin, *Hammer's German Grammar and Usage*, 5th edn. London: Routledge, 2011.
sources.note: §1.2.1, pp. 14–18, on the formation of the plural.

rules.heading: The plural without a change
rules.statement: Masculine and neuter nouns ending in **-er**, **-el** or **-en** keep their form in the plural, and the article alone shows the number.
footnotes: The diminutives in **-chen** and **-lein**, which are neuter whatever they denote (¶29), all belong here: *das Mädchen — die Mädchen*.

sources.citation: Durrell, Martin, *Hammer's German Grammar and Usage*, 5th edn. London: Routledge, 2011.
sources.note: §1.2.1, pp. 14–18, for the unchanged plural of masculines and neuters in -er, -el, -en.

rules.heading: The plural with the Umlaut alone
rules.statement: Many nouns of that same shape take the Umlaut in the plural instead of an ending, so the stem vowel alone carries the number.
footnotes: Only **a**, **o**, **u** and **au** have an Umlaut to take — **ä**, **ö**, **ü**, **äu** (¶2, ¶4, ¶5, ¶11). A stem whose vowel is **e** or **i** cannot be marked this way, which is why *der Lehrer* stands unchanged (¶34).
*die Mutter* and *die Tochter* are the feminine nouns of this class.

sources.citation: Durrell, Martin, *Hammer's German Grammar and Usage*, 5th edn. London: Routledge, 2011.
sources.note: §1.2.1, pp. 14–18, for the umlauted plural without an ending, and *Mutter*, *Tochter* as its feminines.

rules.heading: The plural in -e
rules.statement: A plural is formed by adding **-e**, most often to a masculine or a neuter noun, and the stem vowel stays as it stands.
footnotes: *das Jahr* and *der Tag* both have a stem vowel that could take the Umlaut (¶35); in this class it does not.

sources.citation: Durrell, Martin, *Hammer's German Grammar and Usage*, 5th edn. London: Routledge, 2011.

rules.heading: The plural in -e with the Umlaut
rules.statement: A second body of nouns adds **-e** and takes the Umlaut with it. The class holds masculine nouns and the feminine nouns that form their plural in **-e** at all.
footnotes: A feminine noun of this class always takes the Umlaut. A masculine one may or may not: *der Sohn — die Söhne* beside *der Tag — die Tage* (¶36).

sources.citation: Durrell, Martin, *Hammer's German Grammar and Usage*, 5th edn. London: Routledge, 2011.
sources.note: §1.2.1, pp. 14–18, on the plural in -e with Umlaut, and the feminines of that class.

rules.heading: The plural in -er
rules.statement: A plural is formed by adding **-er**, and the stem vowel takes the Umlaut wherever it can. The class holds neuter nouns and a few masculine ones, and no feminine one.
footnotes: *das Kind* has no Umlaut in the plural because **i** has none to take (¶35), and not because the noun stands outside the class.

sources.citation: Durrell, Martin, *Hammer's German Grammar and Usage*, 5th edn. London: Routledge, 2011.
sources.note: §1.2.1, pp. 14–18, on the plural in -er and the obligatory Umlaut where the vowel admits one.

rules.heading: The plural in -(e)n
rules.statement: A noun ending in **-e**, **-el** or **-er** adds **-n**, and any other noun of this class adds **-en**. It is the plural of almost every feminine noun, and it never takes the Umlaut.
footnotes: A feminine noun in **-in** (¶30) doubles the **n** before the ending: *die Lehrerin — die Lehrerinnen*.

The **-el** and **-er** that take **-n** here are feminine; the masculine and neuter nouns in those same endings stand unchanged instead (¶34). *die Kartoffel — die Kartoffeln* against *der Löffel — die Löffel*.

sources.citation: Durrell, Martin, *Hammer's German Grammar and Usage*, 5th edn. London: Routledge, 2011.
sources.note: §1.2.1, pp. 14–18, on the plural in -(e)n, its predominance among feminines, and the absence of the Umlaut from it.

rules.heading: The plural in -s
rules.statement: A plural is formed by adding **-s**, chiefly to nouns taken from other languages and to shortened forms.
footnotes: The **-s** is written onto the noun without an apostrophe, and the stem is untouched: *die Babys*, not *die Baby's* and not *die Bäbys*.

sources.citation: Durrell, Martin, *Hammer's German Grammar and Usage*, 5th edn. London: Routledge, 2011.
sources.note: §1.2.1, pp. 14–18, on the -s plural and the borrowings that carry it.
Cited for the -s plural as the class of loanwords and abbreviations.

rules.heading: The plural is a property of the noun
rules.statement: Which of the seven formations a noun takes follows neither from its shape nor from its gender, and two nouns alike in both may take different ones. A noun is therefore cited with its plural beside it, as *der Tag, die Tage*.

examples.note: -e with the Umlaut (¶37); same gender, same shape
the Umlaut alone (¶35); both are masculines in -er
-er (¶38); both are neuters of one syllable

footnotes: Gender narrows the choice without settling it: almost every feminine noun takes **-(e)n** (¶39), and no feminine noun takes **-er** (¶38).

sources.citation: Durrell, Martin, *Hammer's German Grammar and Usage*, 5th edn. London: Routledge, 2011.
sources.note: §1.2.1, pp. 14–18: the plural class is lexical, and the citation of a noun carries it.

vocabulary.notes: Unchanged in the plural; only the article moves, from der to die.

drills.stem: Which of these are plurals?
drills.explanation: *Kinder* carries the **-er** of ¶38 and *Autos* the **-s** of ¶40. *Frau* and *Katze* are feminine singulars, where **die** is the article of the gender (¶25) rather than of the plural (¶26).

drills.stem: *die Kartoffel* takes **-n** and *die Frau* takes **-en**. What decides which of the two endings a noun of this class gets?
options: whether the noun already ends in -e, -el or -er
whether the noun has more than one syllable
whether the stem vowel could take the Umlaut
drills.explanation: A noun ending in **-e**, **-el** or **-er** needs only the **-n**; any other takes the full **-en** (¶39). Both nouns here are feminine, so gender settles nothing, and no noun of this class takes the Umlaut at all.

drills.stem: *der Lehrer* names one teacher. Which of these names more than one?
drills.explanation: A masculine noun in **-er** is unchanged in the plural, and the article alone shows the number — *der Lehrer*, *die Lehrer* (¶34, ¶26). *das* is the neuter singular article and cannot mark a plural at all (¶25).

drills.stem: What is the plural of *der Stuhl*?
drills.explanation: *Stuhl* adds **-e** and takes the Umlaut with it (¶37). *die Stuhle* would be the plain **-e** of ¶36, which this noun does not take.

drills.stem: *die Kartoffel* has the plural *die Kartoffeln*, but *der Löffel* has the plural *die Löffel*. What separates them?
options: *Löffel* has an Umlaut already and cannot take an ending
drills.explanation: The ending **-el** is shared, so it cannot be what decides. A feminine noun in -el adds **-n** (¶39); a masculine or neuter one in -el stands unchanged (¶34). The **ö** of *Löffel* belongs to the stem and is not a plural mark (¶35).

drills.stem: Which of these plurals are formed with **-n** or **-en**?
drills.explanation: *Frauen*, *Kartoffeln* and *Katzen* all belong to ¶39, which is the plural of almost every feminine noun. *Häuser* adds **-er** and takes the Umlaut with it (¶38) — a class no feminine noun belongs to, and *Haus* is neuter.

drills.stem: How many of these are plurals? — *die Bücher*, *die Frau*, *die Autos*, *die Katze*, *die Städte*
drills.explanation: *Bücher* (¶38), *Autos* (¶40) and *Städte* (¶37) are plurals. *Frau* and *Katze* are feminine singulars, where **die** is the article of the gender (¶25) and not of the number (¶26).

drills.stem: *die Stadt* has the plural *die Städte*. Which numbered rule governs that formation?
drills.explanation: *Stadt* adds **-e** and takes the Umlaut with it, which is ¶37; a feminine noun of that class always umlauts. ¶36 is the same ending without the Umlaut, and ¶35 the Umlaut without the ending.

drills.stem: What is the plural of *das Baby*?
drills.explanation: A noun taken from another language forms its plural in **-s**, and the stem is untouched (¶40). Nothing in this class takes the Umlaut, so *Bäbys* is not a possible form.

drills.stem: Which of these is not one of the seven ways German forms a plural?
drills.explanation: **-in** builds a feminine noun out of a masculine one (¶30); it changes the sex denoted, not the number. The other three are among the seven (¶33).

drills.stem: Pair each noun with the way it forms its plural.
drills.explanation: *die Lehrer* is unchanged (¶34), *die Äpfel* takes the Umlaut and no ending (¶35), *die Kinder* adds **-er** (¶38), and *die Autos* adds **-s** (¶40). *Lehrer* and *Apfel* are both masculines in -er and -el, which is what the first two pairings trade on; the **e** of *Lehrer* has no Umlaut to take.

drills.stem: *das Buch* becomes *die Bücher* and *das Kind* becomes *die Kinder*. Why does one take the Umlaut and the other not?
options: because **u** has an Umlaut to take and **i** has none
because *Buch* is neuter and *Kind* is masculine
drills.explanation: The **-er** plural takes the Umlaut wherever the stem vowel admits one, and only **a**, **o**, **u** and **au** do (¶38, ¶35). *Kind* has **i**, which has no Umlaut. Both nouns are neuter and both are regular members of the class (¶29).

drills.stem: *der Vogel* forms its plural without adding any ending. What is that plural?
drills.explanation: The stem vowel takes the Umlaut and carries the number by itself (¶35). *die Vogel* would be the unchanged plural of ¶34, which this noun does not take.

drills.stem: Pair each noun with the way it forms its plural.
drills.explanation: *die Frauen* (¶39), *die Häuser* (¶38), *die Wagen* unchanged (¶34), *die Städte* (¶37). *Haus* and *Stadt* both umlaut, which is what the first pairing trades on — the ending is what tells the two classes apart, and no feminine noun takes **-er** at all.

drills.stem: *die Lehrerin* is the feminine of *der Lehrer*. What is its plural?
drills.explanation: A noun in **-in** doubles the **n** and adds **-en** (¶39, ¶30). *der Lehrer* is itself unchanged in the plural (¶34), so the masculine and the feminine look alike in the singular and not in the plural.

drills.stem: **Die Mütter und die Väter warten.** Which of these hold?
options: the **die** in front of *Mütter* shows that the noun is feminine
both nouns form their plural by the Umlaut alone
drills.explanation: *Mutter* and *Vater* both take the Umlaut and no ending (¶35). In the plural all three genders take **die**, so the article says nothing about gender there (¶26) — *Vater* is masculine by its meaning (¶27), and *Mutter* feminine by hers (¶28).

drills.stem: *der Tag* has the plural *die Tage*, and *der Stuhl* has *die Stühle*. Both nouns are masculine, both are one syllable, and both have a stem vowel that can take the Umlaut. What follows?
options: which plural a noun takes is a property of that noun
masculine nouns take -e, and the Umlaut with it is optional
the Umlaut appears on the shorter of two competing forms
*Stühle* is an exception to a rule that *Tage* keeps
drills.explanation: Two nouns alike in gender, in shape and in stem vowel take different formations — *Tage* by ¶36 and *Stühle* by ¶37 — so neither gender nor shape settles the choice (¶41). Nothing marks *Stühle* as the exceptional one; both are ordinary members of their classes.

drills.stem: What is the plural of *das Jahr*?
drills.explanation: *Jahr* adds **-e** (¶36). Its **a** could take an Umlaut (¶35) and in this noun does not, which is what makes *Jähre* look possible.

drills.stem: Which of these are singulars?
drills.explanation: *Mädchen* is unchanged in the plural (¶34), so only the article separates *das Mädchen* from *die Mädchen* (¶26). *die Katze* is a feminine singular (¶25), and *Bücher* is the **-er** plural of *das Buch* (¶38).

drills.stem: **Die Zimmer sind klein.** Which of these hold?
drills.explanation: *das Zimmer* is unchanged in the plural (¶34), so the noun by itself does not say which is meant; **die** does, since the neuter singular takes *das* (¶25, ¶26). A noun of this class adds no ending at all, so *Zimmern* is not one of its forms.

sources.citation: Durrell, Martin, *Hammer's German Grammar and Usage*, 5th edn. London: Routledge, 2011.
